title: Skiff's Silly Sound Surprise
markdown:
At the edge of Whispering Woods lived Skiff, a skunk whose fur was midnight and whose stripes were winter-moon white. At night a worry tickled his whiskers. His special scent was, some evenings, a little much.

“What if everyone runs from our midnight cocoa stand because of my skunkiness?” he whispered to Honey the hamster, while the first stars practised being brave. “What if they sniff and scurry, and the cocoa sits there getting lonely?”

Honey’s paws twitched. Her eyes were shiny black beads. She scampered up his arm and nuzzled his nose. “Your skunkiness is you, Skiff. And we will make the most marshmallowy cocoa in the woods. Too yummy to resist, even for a nose with opinions.”

The idea had arrived on a slanting afternoon, sun on Skiff’s back, Honey mid-sunflower-seed. “A midnight stand,” she had chirped, “when the stars are brightest and the woods go quiet. Warm cocoa. Giant marshmallow clouds. Snowy mountains in a cup.”

Skiff’s worry-whiskers quivered. Happy faces and warm bellies argued back. They found a fallen-log table, a shiny acorn pot, bowls carved from hollow acorns, and a bag of marshmallows as soft as cloud-fluff that insisted on being eaten one at a time for quality.

They set up where the forest path met the meadow. The moon was a thin silver sliver, long shadows practising dance steps of their own. Damp earth. Sweet pine. Skiff stirred while Honey counted marshmallows into a proud little mountain and rejected two for being insufficiently cloudlike. Cocoa smell rose, rich enough to make a shadow lean closer.

Then: rustle, rustle, scritch-scratch from the trees. Then louder: rustle, rustle, thump-thump, as if something heavy had opinions about dancing and had brought its feet.

Mortimer the field mouse peeked from a dewy fern, whiskers on duty. “What’s that noise? It sounds a bit spooky.”

Iestyn Bear, lumbering toward late berries, stopped and sniffed. “Suspicious. Not a normal forest sound.” Fur bristled along his back, a small brown hedge of doubt.

Skiff’s heart tried to be a drum. They think it is scary. They will think I am scary. He pictured empty acorn cups and a stand left talking to itself. His tail tucked. A knot tied itself in his middle.

Honey saw the frown and the tuck. She scurried to the tree-edge, ears up. “Wait. It is not what you think. It is not spooky.”

Skiff followed, still low-tailed, and peeked through a blueberry bush still holding a few late berries like dark lanterns. A family of rabbits: Mama, Papa, three little ones, hopping and twirling, ears like silken scarves, practising a very enthusiastic dance in a ring of flattened grass. They giggled. They counted, lost the count, started again. They stumbled over their own long feet. Rustle-scritch-scratch was only jumping, badly and with joy. One bunny sat down hard and applauded himself.

Honey bounced back to the gathering animals, who had crept closer now that curiosity was beating spooky. “The Cottontail family. They are practising ballet for the Grand Forest Festival next week. The thumps are landings. The scritches are turns.”

Mortimer crept closer, fern-water on his ears. Iestyn let out a gentle huff. “Ballet?” He tilted his big head as if the word might slide off and go look for honey instead.

“Watch.” Honey pointed. The rabbits launched a wobbly pirouette, ears like windmills that had not agreed on a wind. The woodland chuckles came soft, then less soft. The rabbits noticed their audience and bowed, floppy ears sweeping the ground, which finished the argument about fear and started a smaller one about who had bowed lowest.

Skiff’s smile arrived slowly, the way cocoa cools enough to sip. The rustling had been clumsy cheer. He stood taller. Worry-whiskers un-tucked. His tail tried a small wag and liked it.

“And now,” Honey called, “warm midnight cocoa with extra marshmallow clouds?”

Mortimer slurped from a tiny acorn cup, sugar on his whiskers, and asked for a second cloud. Iestyn enjoyed a giant mug and grumbled between sips in the contented way of bears who have decided the night is safe. The Cottontails, after a final grand bow, hopped over for a sweet and left grassy footprints like a second, smaller dance. Skiff served cup after cup, scent and all, and nobody ran. A late moth circled the pot as if it had paid. He had been too busy pouring to rehearse being frightening. The brave feeling was warmer than the pot. He was Skiff the skunk, midnight cocoa server, and the stand smelled of chocolate, pine, and a little of him, which turned out to be the recipe.
